explication:
<explanation>
1. Identify the project type and purpose
   - This is an open-source, interactive prompt-engineering tutorial delivered as Jupyter notebooks.  
   - It supports two “backends” for demos: Anthropic’s Claude via its Python SDK, and AWS Bedrock via boto3.  
   - It includes a CloudFormation template to provision any required AWS resources for a hands-on workshop.

2. Analyze the file structure
   - Top-level modules:
     • AmazonBedrock/      – Jupyter notebooks demonstrating prompt-engineering via AWS Bedrock (boto3).
     • Anthropic 1P/       – Parallel notebooks using Anthropic’s native Python client.
     • cloudformation/     – workshop-v1-final-cfn.yml for deploying AWS stack (e.g., IAM roles, S3 buckets).
     • utils/              – Python package with shared helper functions (hints, wrappers).
     • requirements.txt    – Python dependencies (anthropic, boto3, jupyter, etc.).
   - Patterns:
     • Separation of content (notebooks) from support code (utils).
     • Two interchangeable service-integration layers (Anthropic vs. Bedrock).
   - Deployment files:
     • CloudFormation YAML under cloudformation/ to stand up AWS resources.

3. Examine the README for additional insights
   - The README describes a 9-chapter tutorial plus appendix.
   - It mentions two external LLM endpoints (Claude Haiku and AWS Bedrock).
   - It points users to “start at 01_Basic Prompt Structure” and work through in order.

4. How to create a system-design diagram
   a. Main components:
      • Jupyter Notebook UI (user interface).
      • Python execution environment (kernel) hosting:
        – Tutorial notebooks (AmazonBedrock/ and Anthropic 1P/).
        – utils library (utils/).
        – Requirements & virtual environment (requirements.txt).
      • CloudFormation provisioning (cloudformation/workshop-v1-final-cfn.yml).
      • External services:
        – Anthropic Claude API endpoint.
        – AWS Bedrock endpoint (via boto3).
        – AWS resources created by CFN (e.g., S3 bucket, IAM roles, logging).
   b. Relationships & interactions:
      • User → opens Notebook UI → selects a lesson.
      • Notebook → imports utils → invokes either Anthropic SDK or boto3.
      • boto3 calls Bedrock API → AWS resources (policies, endpoints) created by CFN template.
      • Anthropic SDK calls Claude endpoint directly.
      • Outputs flow back into the notebook for interactive playground.
   c. Architectural patterns / design principles:
      • Modular “backend adapter” layer (Anthropic vs. AWS).
      • Clear separation of content (notebooks) vs. code (utils).
      • Infrastructure-as-Code (CloudFormation) for workshop setup.
   d. Key technologies / frameworks:
      • Jupyter Notebook.
      • Python 3.x, virtualenv.
      • anthropic Python SDK.
      • boto3 (AWS Bedrock).
      • AWS CloudFormation YAML.
      • Optional: S3, IAM, CloudWatch (deployed by CFN).

5. Guidelines for tailoring the diagram to this project
   - Emphasize this is an educational tool, so group all “lesson content” under the Notebook UI.
   - Show two parallel integration flows:
     • Anthropic’s Claude via its SDK.
     • AWS Bedrock via boto3 + CFN-provisioned resources.
   - Illustrate the CFN template as a one-time provisioning step that stands up AWS infra.
   - Show that utils/ is reused by both sets of notebooks.

6. Diagram elements to include
   - Clear labels:
     • Notebook UI
     • Python Kernel & vEnv
     • utils package
     • Anthropic SDK (Claude endpoint)
     • boto3 (Bedrock endpoint)
     • CFN Template → AWS Resources
   - Directional arrows:
     • From Notebook UI → Python Kernel → utils → appropriate SDK.
     • From SDK boxes → External API endpoints → back to notebooks.
   - Color/shapes:
     • Blue boxes for local components (notebooks, utils).
     • Green boxes for external services (Anthropic, AWS).
     • Orange cylinder/cloud shape for AWS resources created by CFN.
     • Dashed arrow to indicate one-time provisioning (CFN → AWS resources).

7. Emphasize level of detail
   - Capture all four layers:
     1. User Interface (Jupyter)
     2. Execution Environment (Python + utils)
     3. Service-Integration Adapters (anthropic vs. boto3)
     4. External Systems (Claude endpoint, AWS infra)
   - Don’t split content notebooks any finer—they can be represented as a grouped module labeled “Tutorial Notebooks.”  
   - Include CFN as a separate provisioning workflow parallel to the notebook runtime.

By following these instructions, you’ll produce a clear, accurate system-design diagram tailored to this tutorial repository, showcasing how interactive notebook content hooks into two LLM backends and an I-a-C provisioning step.
